newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. targets Cuba, Sudan, Serbia at UN rights body. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. targets Cuba, Sudan, Serbia at UN rights body. [CORRECTED 14:50 GMT]

text.p: The United States plans to bring resolutions to the U.N. Human Rights Commission targeting gross violations in Cuba, Sudan and the states of former Yugoslavia, particularly Serbia, U.S. officials said on Thursday.
Washington, expecting hardline Arab countries to present their usual "negative" motions critical of Israel, is likely to offer its own "balanced" motion on the Middle East, they added.

In a speech on Thursday, Former Senator Claiborne Pell, a senior member of the U.S. delegation, urged the U.N.'s main human rights forum to recognise progress in the peace process and said it should stop singling out Israel for harsh treatment.

But the U.S. delegation, led by Nancy Rubin, will take its cues regarding China from the European Union, which has still to make clear whether it will go after Beijing in the 53 member body (corrects from "61-member body"), according to the U.S. officials in Geneva for the talks.
"We need them (the EU) to step forward with a resolution on China before we take steps," a U.S. official told Reuters.
"We still don't have a EU draft resolution in hand yet."

In a speech to the talks on Thursday, Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, speaking for the European Union, named Wei Jingsheng as one of three rights' defenders worldwide who have been silenced. He later told a news conference that the EU had not yet decided whether to present a resolution on China.
For the last six years in a row, Beijing has defeated motions by the EU, co-sponsored by the United States, to have the forum express concern about alleged repression in China.
In its recent annual report on human rights, the U.S. State Department accused Beijing of effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation or exile.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said after a visit to Beijing last month that in the absence of Chinese concessions, Washington would co-sponsor a resolution at the U.N. session.
"Our position is where it was when Mrs Albright left after her visit. We will agree to co-sponsor a resolution on China if the EU comes forward," a U.S. official in Geneva said.

Albright pushed China to sign the two major human rights covenants, guaranteeing civil and political as well as cultural, social and economic rights. A Foreign Ministry spokesman said later that Beijing was considering signing, but gave no date.
China is under U.S. pressure to release detainees with medical conditions and to resume talks with the International Committee of the Red Cross to allow its first prison visits.
"We've been negotiationg with China encouraging respect for human rights all year round -- not just during the Commission," a U.S. official said.
"At this point the response is not adequate," he added. "As we get closer to a vote, China will not make major changes -- that is the reality."
Cuba is again on Washington's hitlist for scrutiny of its "egregious human rights violations", including harassment of rights activists and dissidents, according to U.S. officials.
The United States will also offer a resolution calling for improvement in human rights in Bosnia, Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro), they said.

It will urge Croatia, Serbia and Republika Srpska to hand over people indicted by the Hague-based International Tribunal, set up by the Security Council to punish war crimes committed during the 3-1/2 year Bosnian conflict.
"The vast majority of the 75 indictees are in Republika Srpska," a U.S. official said. These included Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, accused of leading Bosnian Serb atrocities.
The U.S. resolution calls on Belgrade to take steps toward democracy, end pressure on media and halt torture of detainees. It demands an end to violence against non-Serbs in Kosovo.
The United States will again present a resolution to renew the mandate of the U.N. special investigator on Sudan.
"There are credible and disturbing reports of a resurgence of slavery within Sudan and religious persecution of Animists (traditional believers) and Christians," a U.S. official said.
